summary:
My Mini NASA is a browser-based hypercasual game that turns space mission design into something anyone can pick up in seconds. It borrows the walk-carry-upgrade loop of idle-arcade hits like My Mini Mart and puts it inside a small spaceport. Players collect Data Cubes from satellites, turn them into grant money, and produce fuel, parts, research papers, and astronauts. They then load these onto the Launch Pad to meet each mission’s needs.

Every mission is a recipe, not a shopping list. Fuel, power, science, crew, and mass all pull against each other, so more supplies never guarantee success. The right balance does. A successful launch puts another satellite in orbit, which brings in more data and unlocks harder missions, from Earth orbit to the Moon and Mars.

The challenge asks for real engineering trade-offs that students can actually experience. Our answer is a game people play because it’s fun, and they learn mission design along the way.
details:
The core loop has five steps:

  1. Collect data. The Ground Station receives Data Cubes from satellites in orbit.
  2. Get funded. The Grant Office converts cubes into budget.
  3. Produce supplies. The Fuel Plant, Engineering, Research Lab, and Academy turn budget and cubes into fuel, parts, research papers, and astronauts.
  4. Plan and launch. The player carries supplies to the Launch Pad. Each mission shows gauges for fuel, power, science, crew, and mass, plus a success chance.
  5. Reap the reward. A successful launch adds a satellite, which raises data income and unlocks new destinations.

The mission rules come from real relationships:

  • Heavier spacecraft need more fuel, following the ideal rocket equation.
  • Instruments and crew need power.
  • Everything counts toward the launcher’s mass limit.

After each launch, a flight report explains why the mission succeeded or fell short, not just whether it did.

Educational design

Learning is built into play rather than delivered as lectures:

  • Trivia quizzes earn bonus points.
  • Facility cards link each building to real NASA operations and history.
  • Mission requirements are learned through experiment, and short hints explain the reasoning behind each result.

Benefits and impact

  • No installation and no prior knowledge needed. Sessions are short and progress is saved on the device.
  • It shows students how mission elements interact as one system, which is the gap the challenge describes. Topics like orbits, rockets, and instruments are usually taught in isolation.
  • The goal is to make mission design approachable for beginners and youth while keeping trade-offs meaningful for intermediate players.

Creativity

We combined a proven mobile genre with systems-level mission design. In a store game, customers buy your products. In My Mini NASA, the mission consumes them, and its success decides how much the universe “pays” you back in data.

Factors we considered

  • Fun versus realism. We kept a few true relationships rather than a full simulation.
  • Accessibility. Gauges and in-world feedback replace menus and long text.
  • Pacing. Short walking distances and quick early wins.
  • Grounding in NASA resources. CubeSat 101, the Mission Design Lab, Concept Maturity Levels, and the Webb “Build It Yourself” game.
  • Room to grow. Next steps are more missions, constraints, and facilities, plus multiplayer for teams of up to four.

Engineering

My Mini NASA is a browser game built with plain JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3 and no frameworks or game engines. It uses HTML Canvas 2D for all the art and effects, the Web Audio API for live-synthesized music and sound, and localStorage for saves. We used Node.js 22 for testing and the build, Git and GitHub with GitHub Actions for version control and CI, and Cloudflare Pages to host the game at https://mymininasa.wiki.
